catalog_locator: Sec. 3.14.5 'Accent-related lengthening in non-final syllables', pp.174-175 incl. fn.207-209; basic rule sec. 2.4.3 'Accent placement' p.63; also sec. 1.5.1.1 'Final accent and consequences' p.35 and the 'Accent' paragraph p.86.
catalog_quote: In the Shirongol languages the accent normally falls on the last syllable. This also applies to Eastern Yugur, although predictable deviations occur under some phonetic circumstances (see 3.14.5.). [p.63] ... [pp.174-175] The default accent placement is on the last syllable. This is found in stems containing only short non-high vowels such as al'tan (*altan) ‘gold’, hele'ɣen (*heligen) ‘liver’, and in stems containing only short high vowels, such as pə'čəg (*bičig) ‘writing’, xəmə'sən (*kïmusun) ‘nail’. However, if the stem contains a contraction length or diphthong, that will take the accent (vowel height is irrelevant), e.g. ǰɔ'rɔ: (*ǰïroa) ‘ambler’, tɔlɔ'ğɔi (*tolagaï) ‘head’; dʉ're: (*döree) ‘stirrup’, du'la:n (*dulaan) ‘warm’, xa'ru:l- (*karïul-) ‘to reply’, but 'ki:re (*keere) ‘outdoors’, 'ǰe:ren (ǰeeren) ‘Mongolian gazelle’. If the stem contains long vowels only, the accent will fall on the final one. If the stem contains short high and non-high vowels, the final accent will be on the last syllable if that has a non-high vowel. If ə is in the final syllable of a disyllabic stem, the accent will avoid the ə, and fall on the vowel of the first syllable in, as in 'ġatən (*katun) ‘empress’, 'xɔ:nə (*konïn) ‘sheep’. In trisyllabic and longer stems, the accent will fall on the rightmost non-high vowel available, as in he'nesən (*hünesün) ‘ash’, 'belwəsən (*belbisün) ‘widow’, ǰə'ğasən (*ǰagasun) ‘fish’, xulă'ğaičə (*kulagaïčï) ‘thief’.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent is final by default (al'tan, hele'ɣen, pə'čəg, xəmə'sən). Deviations are predictable from vowel length/quality: a long vowel or diphthong anywhere in the stem takes the accent ('ki:re, 'ǰe:ren; if several long vowels, the last one); in stems mixing schwa (< short high vowels) with full non-high vowels the accent avoids a final-syllable schwa and falls on the rightmost non-high vowel ('ġatən 'empress', 'xɔ:nə 'sheep', he'nesən 'ash', 'belwəsən 'widow'), often lengthening it. Junast 1981:14 (per fn.207) and Chinese handbooks state only the basic rule: stress on the last syllable, moving rightward onto vowel-bearing suffixes (gələd, gələd'le, gələdle'sen); stress is not distinctive.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress in any source seen.
new_statements.exceptions: Long vowels/diphthongs attract accent regardless of position ('ki:re, 'ǰe:ren vs du'la:n); accent retracts off final schwa onto rightmost non-high vowel ('ġatən, 'xɔ:nə, 'belwəsən; Nugteren 2003 snippet: 'accent also tends to flee the final syllable if it contains i, as in xuucin, belwisin'); Malov/Kotwicz mark initial accent in a few words (e.g. *hodun 'star'); in Baoan-type QG languages Arabic/Chinese loans may have non-final accent (sec. 1.5.1.1, general QG remark).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level accent, described on stems in citation form; per fn.208 (Bolčuluu & Jalsan 1990:143) long suffix vowels take over the accent ('xɔ:nə > acc./gen. xɔ:'ni:n, refl. xɔ:nə'ya:n) while short-vowel suffixes leave it on the stem (dat. 'xɔ:nədə); Junast 1981: accent moves rightward as vowel-bearing suffixes are added. Accent is stated to be non-distinctive (county gazetteer/Junast: 重音虽不区别词义).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Eastern (Shira) Yugur = Glottolog east2337 (ISO yuy), the Mongolic language of Sunan Yugur Autonomous County, Gansu (Chinese 东部裕固语, also 'Enger'); not to be confused with Western (Sarig) Yugur west2402, a Turkic language (Roos 2000 in the Glottolog list describes west2402, not this language). Bolčuluu & Jalsan's data are mainly from the Kangle area dialect per Nugteren 2011; Junast 1981 likewise Kangle.

tone.quote: This is due to the fact that the stress of Mongolian words usually falls on first syllable, and phonetic realization of a target vowel varies according to its position in a word. However, as a Mongolic language, Eastern Yugur language has been in close contact and under great influences of Western Yugur language (Turkic), the stress has shifted to the final syllable. This stress shift results in vowel reduction or elision in initial syllable: “basa” → “pəsa”(again, also), “bayan” → “bəyan” (rich) ...
